notes.meaning: God speaks with biting sarcasm, pretending that Job must understand all these mysteries because he was alive when the world was created. In truth, Job was not yet born and knows very little of what took place before his time. This gentle teasing humbles Job by showing that human life is far too brief to grasp the eternal plans of God.

God pictures snow and hail as if they were stored in vast heavenly warehouses until He chooses to call them forth. He keeps these storms ready for times of trouble and battle, using them as instruments of judgment against His enemies, as He did in the days of Joshua. A man who cannot even visit such storehouses has no right to question the Almighty who commands them.

God asks how the light is distributed over the earth and how the fierce east wind is scattered. Both light and wind move so swiftly and widely that no person can track or control their journeys. This reminds Job that daily wonders occur beyond human calculation.

God asks who cuts out a channel in the sky for heavy rainstorms or clears a path for the lightning bolt. Torrents of rain and lightning flashes do not travel at random; God steers every drop and spark with exact care. Since Job cannot govern a single storm, he cannot govern God's moral rule of the world.

God pours rain onto barren deserts where no human beings live or farm. He does this to refresh the lonely wasteland and cause tender grass to sprout for wild creatures. This reveals that God's loving care reaches across creation and does not exist merely to serve human needs.

God asks whether the rain has a human father or who gives birth to drops of morning dew. No mortal can produce a shower of rain or generate dew by his own power. God alone produces moisture to sustain life on the earth.

God asks what womb brought forth ice and frost from heaven. When intense cold arrives, fluid water freezes as hard as stone, locking up the surface of the deep. Humans can only marvel at this great transformation that only the Creator can accomplish.

God asks if Job can fasten the cluster of stars called the Pleiades or unbind the belt of Orion. The Pleiades constellation was linked with the delightful arrival of spring, while Orion was connected with the cold storms of winter. Job is powerless to alter the seasons or control the movements of the night sky.

God asks whether Job can bring out the constellations in their right seasons or guide the Great Bear and her cubs across the heavens. The regular movement of the stars through the months happens on God's timetable, not man's. Job must acknowledge that he cannot steer the heavenly bodies.

God asks if Job knows the fixed laws that rule the heavens, and whether he can establish their influence over the earth. The sun, moon, and stars affect earthly weather and seasons because God ordained their paths. Since humans cannot direct the sky, they cannot run the universe better than God.

God asks if Job can shout an order to the clouds and make a downpour of rain cover him. If a man tries to command the clouds, they will not obey his voice. We depend entirely on God for the rain that nourishes our crops.

God asks if Job can dispatch lightning bolts and have them report back like obedient servants saying, 'Here we are.' Terrifying lightning strikes obey God's commands instantly, but they will never answer to a human master. True authority over nature belongs to the Lord alone.

God asks who planted wisdom deep inside man and gave understanding to the human mind. The ability to think, reason, and perceive truth is a gift directly from the Creator. Since all human intelligence comes from God, no person can ever claim to be wiser than Him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars translate the unusual Hebrew terms as storm clouds and meteors rather than the human mind, meaning that even weather phenomena display God's wise ordering.

notes.meaning: God asks who has the wisdom to count the clouds or tip over the skies' water jars to pour down rain. When dry ground turns into hard lumps, rain softens the soil, yet God knows exactly when to stop the shower so the earth is not flooded. Man can neither produce rain nor close the clouds when too much water falls.

God turns to the animal kingdom and asks if Job can hunt food for a hungry lioness and her cubs. Young lions crouch inside their dens and wait in thickets for food that only God provides. God demonstrates His great care by feeding even dangerous predators that man cannot tame.

God asks who supplies food for the raven when its hungry chicks wander and cry out. Though humans often look down on the raven as an unclean or unpleasant bird, God treats the cries of its young as a prayer to Him and provides what they need. If God faithfully cares for the hungry young of a despised bird, His people can be sure He will care for them.
